slides.title: Principle and source
bullets: α-Amylase hydrolyses 2-chloro-4-nitrophenyl-α-D-maltotrioside (CNPG3), releasing 2-chloro-4-nitrophenol (CNP) (10 CNPG3 → 9 CNP + CNPG2 + maltotriose + glucose).
The rate of CNP formation (405 nm) is proportional to α-amylase activity.
Amylase comes mainly from the pancreas and salivary glands; it is used to diagnose and follow acute and chronic pancreatitis.

This protocol follows, as an example, the instructions for use of the SPINREACT “Amylase-LQ” kit (IFU BEIS27-I, 07/06/16). The IFU of your laboratory’s own kit always takes precedence: other kits may use different volumes, times, factors and reference values.

slides.title: Specimen, reagents and equipment
bullets: Specimen: serum or plasma (heparin is the recommended anticoagulant), separated from the cells quickly; adjust urine to pH ≈ 7.0 before storage. Stable 1 month at 2–8 °C.
Reagent: MES pH 6.0 100 mmol/L, CNPG3 2.25 mmol/L, sodium chloride 350 mmol/L, calcium acetate 6 mmol/L, potassium thiocyanate 900 mmol/L, sodium azide 0.95 g/L.
Equipment: spectrophotometer or analyser reading at 405 nm, 37 °C thermostat, 1.0 cm cuvettes.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The reagent is ready to use (single reagent).
After opening: stable for 60 days at 2–8 °C if capped immediately after each opening.
Only 37 °C: amylase activity is temperature-dependent — below or above 37 °C results appear falsely lower or higher.

slides.title: Reagent preparation (for a semi-automatic analyser)
bullets: The values come from the SPINREACT “Amylase-LQ” IFU (BEIS27-I). The IFU of the kit you use and the analyser manual always take precedence — check the programme against them.

slides.title: Procedure (manual, per the IFU)
bullets: 1. Conditions: wavelength 405 nm; constant temperature 37 °C.
2. Use a 1 cm cuvette; zero the instrument with distilled water.
3. Pipette into a cuvette: reagent 1.0 mL + serum/plasma 20 µL (urine — 10 µL).
4. Mix and wait 30 seconds.

slides.title: Procedure (manual, per the IFU)
bullets: 5. Read the initial absorbance (A), start the stopwatch and read every 1 minute for 3 minutes.
6. Calculate the absorbance differences and the mean change per minute (ΔA/min).

slides.title: Semi-automatic analyser: amylase programme
rows: Initial A, then every 1 min for 3 min

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: Serum or plasma: α-amylase (U/L) = ΔA/min × 3954; urine: ΔA/min × 7908.
Conversion: U/L × 0.01667 = µkat/L.
Linear up to 2200 U/L; above that, dilute the sample 1/2 with NaCl 9 g/L and multiply the result by 2.
IFU reference: serum or plasma up to 90 U/L; urine up to 450 U/L.

slides.title: Calculation and result
bullets: These values are for orientation; each laboratory should establish its own reference range.

slides.title: Interferences and errors
bullets: Haemolysis interferes. Chelating agents such as citrate and EDTA inhibit amylase.
Saliva and sweat contain amylase: never mouth-pipette and avoid skin contact with the reagent or ware.
Drugs and other interfering substances are listed in the literature (IFU — Young DS).
IFU: performance depends on the analyser used.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: Assayed control sera are run with each series (IFU: SPINTROL H Normal and Pathologic).
If a control falls outside its range, check the instrument, reagents and technique; do not release patient results.
Each laboratory sets its own quality-control scheme and the corrective actions when controls are out of tolerance.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: The reagent contains potassium thiocyanate: avoid inhalation, skin or eye contact; if it happens, wash with plenty of water and see a doctor. It also contains sodium azide.
Serum and plasma are potentially infectious: wear gloves and never pipette by mouth.
Follow the precautions in the IFU and the safety data sheet (SDS) when handling the reagents.
Used cuvettes, tubes and tips are disinfected.
